text: Welcome to Statistics and Probability for Data Science, step three of the Data Scientist path. You've already learned to pull data with SQL and manipulate it with Python. This course answers the question that comes next: once you have the data, what can you honestly conclude from it? No prior statistics is assumed — we build every idea from plain-language intuition, then check it with short code you can run yourself.

Statistics is the discipline of learning from data while being honest about uncertainty — that last phrase is the whole point. Computing an average is easy; knowing how much to trust that average is the skill that separates a data scientist from someone with a calculator. Statistics does three jobs: describe what you have, infer something about a larger group you didn't fully observe, and quantify how sure you are, using probability.

A population is the complete group you care about — every order your company will ever receive. A sample is the part of that group you actually measured. Nearly all real analysis is done on samples, because measuring everything is expensive or impossible. Let's invent a population of 10,000 order values, then pretend we can only afford to look at 50 at a time.

The population mean comes out to 60.44. Sampling just 50 orders three separate times gives means of 60.7, 58.77, and 58.38 — three different answers, and none of them equals the true 60.44. Nobody made a mistake. This is sampling variability: every sample is a slightly different random slice of the population. In real work you never see the true population mean — you see one sample mean and must decide how far to trust it.

Data science decisions rest on statistical claims: the new checkout page increases conversion, this model is better than the last one, customers in this region spend more. Without statistics you can't tell a real effect from an ordinary wobble caused by sampling. Statistics gives you the vocabulary and the tools to say this is probably real, or we cannot tell yet.

Here's the road ahead: descriptive statistics first — types of data, center, spread, shape, and charts. Then probability — the math of chance, conditional probability, and Bayes' theorem. Then distributions and sampling, hypothesis testing — a disciplined way to decide between a real effect and just noise — and finally correlation, experiments, and a full capstone analysis from start to finish.

A note on honesty: the datasets in this course are small and illustrative, chosen so you can see every number, but the habits transfer directly to real, messy data. To recap: statistics describes data, infers from samples to populations, and quantifies uncertainty. Samples vary, so a single sample statistic is an estimate, not the truth. Next, we look at the different kinds of data you'll meet, because the kind of data decides which statistics make sense.
